connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I am a citizen in the United states but I came as a legal immigrant in 2011
micronarrative: The “No one is illegal” banner stops me first—it mirrors my own story. I grew up in Iraq, where war made survival a daily act of will. When I came here, language was a bridge: I’d always been drawn to English, and though my first language is Arabic, I learned it quickly. Back home, education was free and open to all, regardless of wealth. That accessibility—alongside my own resilience forged in instability—shaped how I see immigration debates. The tension in that town hall? I recognize it. Being an immigrant means navigating conflict, whether in war-torn cities or public spaces where people shout over each other. The phrase “No one is illegal” carries weight for me because I’ve lived the reality of being labeled, of crossing borders—both geographic and linguistic—and knowing that survival often depends on community, not division.
